newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin meets Netanyahu, sees better Israel ties.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin meets Netanyahu, sees better Israel ties.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, greeting Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in the Kremlin on Tuesday, said he expected economic and political ties between the two countries to expand significantly.

"Our countries and their leaders have finished a period of biased attitudes and have energetically moved toward each other," Interfax news agency reported Yeltsin as saying. "This regards political, economic and trade relations."
He said that trade between the two countries -- which Israeli officials said is about $500 million annually -- "with good will on both sides could increase significantly".
On the agenda for Netanyahu, paying his first visit to Moscow since becoming prime minister nine months ago, were discussions on trade links and Russia's role in Middle East peace talks.
Under fire at home and abroad for his troop redeployment plan for the West Bank, the Israeli leader has made clear he wants to focus on bilateral economic issues.

"Israel is prepared to cooperate with Russia economically. We have a great future together," Netanyahu told reporters at the elegant Metropol hotel where he was the dinner guest of Moscow mayor Yuri Luzhkov on Monday.

"Israel is fast becoming the Silicon Valley of the eastern hemisphere. We have more scientists per capita than any other country," he said, adding that many of these scientists were of Russian origin and could be a bridge to greater cooperation.

More than 650,000 Jews have moved to Israel from the former Soviet Union since Moscow flung open the doors to emigration in 1989 in an era of glasnost (openness). Netanyahu's government includes several prominent former Russians, including former Soviet Jewish dissident Natan Sharansky.
"We have a million people who speak Russian," Netanyahu said on Monday. "That is the greatest concentration outside the former Soviet Union."
Moscow only re-established long-severed ties with Israel in 1991 for the launch of Arab-Israeli peace talks in Madrid co-sponsored by the United States and the then-Soviet Union.
Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov, an Arabic speaker with long experience of the Middle East, is keen to revive Moscow's influence in the region, much reduced by Russia's economic woes.
Later on Tuesday Netanyahu is scheduled to meet Primakov, Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, Russian businessmen and members of Moscow's Jewish community.

His 48-hour visit, which coincides with mounting tension between Israeli soldiers and Palestinians on the West Bank, follows a similar trip to Moscow by Palestinian President Yasser Arafat last month.
In Soviet times Moscow was a strong supporter of Palestinian self-rule, helping to balance Washington's pro-Israel stance.
Israel wants Moscow to use its influence to persuade Syria, one of the Jewish state's arch-enemies, to resume peace talks.

One issue overshadowing Netanyahu's visit concerns reports of Russian sales of advanced military technology to Iran. Netanyahu said last week he would press Russia not to help Tehran develop ballistic missiles.

Last month the Los Angeles Times said U.S. intelligence reports indicated Russia had given Iran technology for the Russian SS-4 missile, which has a range almost three times greater than that of any missile now in Tehran's arsenal. Moscow denied the report.
The late Yitzhak Rabin made the first visit of an Israeli prime minister to Moscow in 1994.
